blocks.x: Yeah, okay, this is the fourth reel, Don Albert, May the 27th, 1972.

Okay, we were talking about, you had to read the poems. The band, as I told you previously, the musicians in those days, they played music. There weren't too many Finnish musicians that had learned music. So when Tra would get these jobs in these nightclubs that required music to be played for the performers such as.

Okay, let's see. Okay, let's see. Okay, and we're at 910 Royal. We're at my apartment where we're sitting and relaxing, and we're just going to chat about jazz. The first thing I wanted to talk about was when you were coming up, what were some of the centers of jazz? What did you think of as being places where there was a lot of jazz?

Well, there was a lot of it. Well, not too many places when I first started in my music career, even when I started learning. But I thought maybe possibly you would want to know the time of my birth, and we'd bring it up to that, and we'd get those questions. Oh, I thought we got on your birth before. I don't know if we did that, Dick. Yeah, okay. I know I was born at 1719 North Robeson here in the old French quarters, and the house still remains there. My daddy lived in there, and I was born in there, and my brothers and sisters were born in there. And the house still stands, and my brother, the young one, is still living there where we lived. What's his name? His name is Leo. He's the last one.
I never have met him.

I don't think you have. He's one of these latecomers. He's born just about the time that my mother was in a change of life. I think she was about 47, so you can understand what type of fella he is. He's a lovable little fella, but he has his own ways, I imagine, like everybody else. And I checked over my, I usually do, check over my residence where I was born yesterday to bring back a few of the memories when I was a little kid, and someday I want to take you over there so we can go through these things.
Yeah, we'll get a cassette machine and do it.

Yeah, fine. And, well, from there, my daddy was a singer and a violin player. I couldn't stand the violin. I tried it, but that was out of question. So I took up singing, as I told you a lot of times in our interviews. And from there, I went to learn the horn, the music first, and then the horn from Milford Pierron, who was the brother of the violin player. And then after I learned from him how to blow the horn, I got pretty good, and I went to take a job with Bigfoot Phillips. And he told me I learned enough from him, I didn't have to go any further. So that's where I began, that's here in New Orleans. Was there much music in New Orleans that you listened to? Not quite as much as it is now, and it was a different type of day and time in music. In those days, music was played. Well, the guys made a living out of it, but to them it was joy and happiness. And just to get to play the music and make other people happy, that was the aim in these old musicians' lives. Of course, they got paid, but the little Paulson wouldn't have liked to hear the bass of what these guys want today for playing music, which I can agree, it's a living, and it's an artistry, and you should be paid for your artistry, not the condemning of all that. I'm just trying to make a little comparison, as you asked me, in those days and the days now. The music was beautiful because it was what the guys were feeling. It was soulful.
Well, who did you listen to come?

Well, Manuel Perez lived across the street from my grandfather, and he was part of the family. And there was another old trumpet player that I very seldom hear too much said about, George Moret. And his wife practically helped my mother to bring me up because that's how close-knit all families were here. All of the Creole families down in this area, they're close-knit. And half the time, my mother couldn't find me. I was either at Old Man Jaws Bowl by my grandfather, by Manuel Perez, all over to Bonnie's house, with Bonnie Bigel, who was his first cousin. And I'd be in one of those places. And you asked me who did I listen to. Well, I used to go out to West End long years ago when he had just nothing but dance halls out there to listen to old George Moret play. And also Manuel. I followed Manuel in the parades, and sometimes I walked the parades with him and carried us home.
Were you any kind of Moret or Parade?

Well, not related to Moret, but to true family ties, yes. But I understand that my grandfather claimed a relationship with Manuel Perez, but what it was right now, I can't remember, but it wasn't close enough for me to be associated as a close relative.
Where was your grandfather from?

From what we understand and what we know from the Dominican Republic, derived the name Dominic Cutter-Hugh off of it. And I understand that his grandfather was Dominic Hugh, the pirate on the gene defense ship. Which is all authentic, because there's a lady died here just a few years ago. That was a close cousin, Miss Tomatis, and she told me about my grandfather's grandfather. How do you spell Tomatis? T-O-T-H-O-M-A-T-I-S.
I never heard of that name before. So they came up from the Dominican Republic?

Dominican Republic, as far as I can go back. I try to search my family tree when I come here, but there's not too many of the old relatives here that can sit down, and they don't want to discuss it. There's a lot of it, they claim it's shady background, to me it's not shady. It's just the way that these old people carried themselves in an aristocratic way, even though they were poor, poor people. And their heritage was rich, and their retainer is such. And they don't want to discuss with the youngsters about their family tree. But I do have a lot of information that was given to them.

Well, you know, it always struck me that so many people here came up from maybe in the Dominican Republic, Santa Domingo, whatever you want to call it. That's right, that's right. The revolution down there sent so many people to various places, they ended up in New Orleans.

Well, yes, but not only the revolution, the New World, the dreams of what was in the New World brought these diverse people over here. And naturally, Dominic, you being a part of the piracy days on the ship's ride, I imagine he would leave his family alone, his family's, to meet him around in that way ever he was going to be.
I think he's buried.

He's buried in the second graveyard on St. Louis in Claymore. It's a little grave there. He has a marker on it. Someone takes care of it, but I don't know who. It's always spotless. But I think it's the Masons. He was a Mason.
Well, we can ask Buddy, the sextant over there. Do you know Buddy?
I don't think he does. I've inquired a couple times, but he wasn't too free with his information.
Well, you know, he was a friend of Buddy Petit's and all the musicians, that guy. Who's this? The sextant over there
called Buddy Huntsman. Well, he knew everybody because it's a burial garden. Yeah, well, naturally,
he would know all the existence of the burial.
Sure.
Yeah, well, he knew. He knows the families and he seems to keep up with people.
Well, maybe sometime when we come back to New Orleans and spend a week or two and we'll research some of this and see what we can come up with. I believe it's a beautiful background.
And I know some of the librarians and actually work in the library. So we can go around and see the label. Right.
And that would kind of clarify my mind as to who I am.
Yeah. Well, you know who you are. Yeah. Not really. You don't know where your family's from. Right.

So that means you don't know who you are. Yes, I know I'm Don Allen. Where, who is Don Allen? Where did he come from? Who's his people? Well, you find a lot of them here. Yet, of course, the family was such a vast family. The McKenna's was my grandmother's people. And the Torriganus was a part of my grandfather. But there's so many branches of these. There's various names that come to your mind. Each family had children, lots of children. They had a lot of children. So naturally, these things spread just like wild grass.
Well, Uncle, your Uncle Natty.
Uncle Natty in Chicago?
Yeah, he said it was Italian.
Who? What's Italian? My uncle doesn't always talk. No. No, indeed.
No Italians.
Well, there were Italians around here. But listen, Italians spell their name differently. They spell it D-O-N-I-C or C-K. But he has a Q-U-E.
Yeah.

Well, you know, sometimes my uncle, he doesn't like to talk to me. That's another one of these things that I'm referring to. He doesn't discuss his background. Yeah. If you've ever talked to him, you'll find that he has a good. Yeah, well,
I never had a maiden. Somehow, just almost happened.
But what about your wife?
What's her name now? Let's get it all right.
Her maiden name was Geringer. G-U-E-R-I-G-E-R. The people around here say Geringer. That's the French way of saying it. But the English way is Geringer.
But what's her full name?
Hazel. Hazel Augustine Geringer.
And she calls herself Dominique.
Well, she calls herself Mrs. Dominique. A lot of people address her as this is Mrs. Dominique.
Yeah.

So, sometimes it becomes confusing. But everybody who knows, I know, have one in San Antonio. There's no problem now because they still call me Don Albert. And that's out of telephone. The name is listed in the telephone. It's Don Albert. Don Albert. So, some of these guys are traveling through the state and they want to see me. They look up at Albert Dominique which they're not going to find me anymore. But they'll find my son's name. And they'll call his number and get my name.
Oh, I see. So, well, now, where you were going is near St. Bernard Avenue.
It's two blocks from St. Bernard. One long block.
What was that street like when you were growing up?

It's the same way now as it was then. There's no difference. I looked at all the old houses yesterday. There has been no improvement. Maybe just a paid job. But it's the same identical way it's always been. And that's over 64 years.
Did you play on that street?

Sure, I played. It was an old hall called the Frans Amie Hall which is about a block, a full block from where I was born. And I used to love to go there because I'd climb up the steps and go to the bands used to play up the stairs that weren't in the pianos. And I would go up there and sit down with Amanda Perez and sometimes it'd be Chris Kelly or all the new railroad runners. Whatever band was there, I was able to get in because everybody knew me and called me but I was this little fella down with the little creole he was coming in and just letting in. I guess I've always been a lack of a fella and I have always been able to make friends on the spur of the moment. There's no problem for me to meet a man today and become closely acquainted with him as a friend.
Have you ever been shy in your life?

Have I ever been shy? Yeah. The whole lot. Well, not shy but been afraid. Been afraid for a few times in my life. During my musical career after I got my band because I'm I'm glad we jumped in the gun now a little bit but I would like to to answer the question about being shy. No, I had no reason to be shy. I guess maybe I'm crazy that's what they say but I was no reason to be shy but afraid, yes. I could go in the woods by myself I'd go meet my daddy at Lake Punch and Train two o'clock in the morning go through the woods walk by myself had no fear of nothing and go out there and meet his friends and be right along with them until I knew I was just a little kid. Well, I've never been shy.
Well, tell me more about your backyard.

Well, I think we're going to have to go and look at this thing. It's amazing. I had a dream that my yard was an immense yard that I had to play in and when I went there yesterday and I looked at it it's the same way it was when I was a kid and I had a picture taking a lot of wash tubs with my horn when I was eight years old and there's no difference in the house and the yard but it's just about the size of a matchbox. Well, you know,
to me one of the beautiful things about the areas around St. Bernard is that you still have the nice houses.
Well, I can...
Oh, that's okay? No, we're just talking. So, I'll see you next week. Yes, all right. I'm getting his life started. Oh, I see. I see. So he's telling me all that.
Yeah, I guess. Will y'all be being pizza saying no more and they want to meet around here knocking, babe?
It was a nice noise. Let's see you later.
Oh, right.
Okay. Anyway, you know, those houses and everything, to me, everything is beautiful except for what they've done to play banana.

That really, you know, that's one of the dreams of my my boyhood days. I remember those great big massive acorn trees. Well, they're old trees. We called them acorn trees. And those were beautiful days for us to play. It was a playground for the poor Negro kids, which I am. And I look at that experience and gee whiz, what a change. There used to be a circle up there on the sand and all in Clevemont. We used to call it the circle. And it was a big palm tree going into this thing. And it all sat around on this cement circle. I didn't sit there until time to go home and exchange stores. But all all of that is gone. Were there a lot of
cars out there?

No cars. Cars were almost a thing in the past. They were just beginning to come in. I'm going back to the horse and the buggy days. Because the salmon oil market is now what the circle market is. Well, there's as much difference in that market there and the market that I'm referring to as daylight and darkness. This is a modern superstore as they call it. And the salmon oil market, the butchers had their stalls. And the vegetable vendors had their stalls. And the fish vendors had their their section set aside for that. And the same token, the poultry people. Each individual had his own. And on the outside of the market was a baby old water trough where the horses used to come to drink. Well, we'd wait until the fresh water come in before the horses got there. And we'd be working around, the kids working around and helping the people get their stands up and get to drink before the horse leaves. Yeah. Yeah. Well,
that's like the cowboys though, you know, they drink downstream for the water.
That's right. They have a reason for it because sometimes a horse has been working kind of hard and he has a slam or something coming out of his mountain, you avoid that.
Well, anyway, was the market closed in or was it open? Oh, it was wide open. You had no walls or nothing?
Oh, you mean as an enclosure? Yeah. Oh, no,
no,
no, no, it was enclosed on the side and they had entrances on the three sides and then there was a place behind it that
the

family. They and that Creole Fiesta Association. We were close to them, to the Demasiata. And, of course, I used to go and get my daddy out and bring him home sometime. I was about eight, nine years old. And then I'd work in the market and help the fellas get their stands ready and I'd get paid with maybe an apple or orange. That was my pay. Well,
what what was your daddy like? You say he was a musician? Was he a no, not professional? Not professional? Just for fun.

He was a cigar maker by trade. My daddy traveled to various parts of the country making cigars familiar. But he also had a great voice. And my grandfather's son, my grandmother sang also. I had a lot of uncles who played music.
You want to shut an awful minute?
Yeah.
Talking about your uncles. Yeah, well, there was

one named Wilson, Wilson Dominick. He played in those days the cornet. And that's Uncle Nat his oldest brother. He was even older than my, no, I think my daddy was the oldest and he was next. But he was killed. A bunch of guys jumped on him after a job uptown. And that was the end of him. And I had another uncle that was a great volumist. And in those days there wasn't a cue for tuberculosis. and he passed away with that a real young man. Of course, I think my grandmother must have had about 10, 12, 14 children. Do you remember all their names? Well, not all of them. Because the son that were dead, they didn't even want to refresh the memory of what happened to them, so they wouldn't tell us who they were.
Which one was the volumist?
His name was, well, they say Naval, but it's Naval, N-A-V-A-L, but the Creole and French would say Naval.
Naval. Naval. Well, now, what was your mother's maiden name? Did you
tell her? My mother's maiden name was, my mother's maiden name was Ratliff, R-A-T-L-E-F-F.
And her first name? George Henry. George Anna Wright, I thought, see. And then the Begards and the Pirones are on, and I can't keep it all straight. Well, no,

I told you that was going to be complicated. The Begards are on the McKenna side. Bonnie's mother was my grandmother's sister. There were five sisters and about four or five brothers. So, after the sisters married, you have the Marqueses that come in there. That's another sister. So, it would take us two, three months to sit down here and go through each individual's married life and their offspring. But that's how Bonnie and I are cousins because my grandmother and his mother were sisters. And Bonnie was born, I think, just, I think his mother was passed away after Bonnie was born. Did you
know Emil, his father? Emil, the girl?
I think that's... On his father? Well, no. No, Bonnie's father is Alec. Alec.
That's right. Emil was the uncle. Yeah. I get a mixed up.
He was a cigar maker
with my
daddy.
And he was a violin player too, but I don't know if he played in your time.
Not professionally. Not
professionally. And you said the de Mausoliere family. I didn't get that straight.
Now, what did
they do?
Well, he used to run those joints around. The alley. The alley. And there was one across the street on Claiborne that's the Martyrera there now. Louisiana?
No, it's Gettison Moss, isn't it? Well, wait a minute. There's the Louisiana, the Rhodes.
No, no, you go back now to Claiborne and Salernon on the other side. That's Gettison really something.
Well, that fellow we were talking to today, he works in Laud. Yes,
he's on Claiborne and Emmett.
He works at Laud.

With Laud. That's right. That's his mother's place. We talk about Asano. She was married to Asano and then she married Emil Laud. And now she's married to George Lopez. The first two months was the past.
Well, anyway, what was back there where the mortuary is?

All these what they called saloons in those days. A guy named Zemo used to run. Great big fellas about six feet five in those days. I couldn't remember him well. Of course, my daddy frequented those places a lot of times. I had to go and get my daddy out. Time to come home.
Well, he didn't drink, did he?
My daddy didn't? If he didn't, I don't know what you call it. He didn't go to work on a Monday. He was catching up from Friday, Saturday, and Sunday.
Did he work on Friday?
Sometimes a half a day. He came home and got started from that. And Monday he had to recuperate and go away Tuesday.
So he'd work about three and a half days. Something like that. Did he make a good living out of that?
Well, I guess he made enough to keep some bread and meat in the house. That's about all I can remember about that. Never knew excess money about the house. That was nothing like that.
And what about your schooling?

Oh, I went to school. I attended Catholic school when I was at Bar at St. Francis is on Bill and Maroney. And of course I used to go to Maroney school. It was a block around there just to be with the kids and the teachers seemed to like me and I could go into rooms. and then after I left Catholic school I went to Jones school which is on Annette and Galvest but there was also a part of the school we used to call it Bucket of Blood. It was an old long house with a bunch of rooms in it. And I don't know why they gave the name of Bucket Blood but that's what we went for our first second and third grade and then when we launched the school we went to Jones school I was transferred from Birold school to Joseph A. Craig and of course from there I was going to Strait University and I used to go to everybody.
What was Strait University now?
Well Strait University now I understand that there's two colleges joined in together Strait was one of them and New Orleans I think was the other which is now Dillon it's those schools that
really. did you study that very long or what did you come to? I
didn't study too long. I had learned how to play music and I decided I wanted to do all of this and so that's what I did.
You weren't in college really?

No but over my travels I've been able to acquire quite a bit of knowledge through various people that I had contacts with professors directors I've done a lot of stage work and it's active besides my music and that way I think that I've acquired enough knowledge to consider that I know what the college education is.
you have a high school degree?
Yes.
You have the high school degree and you're really self-educated on a college level. I think so.
That's what I can say.
Do you like to read?
Oh I love to read. I read everything I possibly can.
Well what about your family? How do they feel about people? Different kinds of people.

Well the old tradition around here has changed considerably but there always was that bridge between families. The old feud and families then into the some didn't like the dark complected ones, the dark complected ones, but vice versa. They didn't like the brides or the whites. It was always. As far as I'm concerned this racial problem has always been. It has always been the same thing. The hatred seems to be instilled in people in this. I don't know whether I can truthfully say that time is going to eliminate that. I doubt seriously that. It's always going to be that element that is going to be retained within a fellow about hatred or animosity against someone else. If it's something he doesn't like about the fellow, he is going to hold that against it.
I find a lot of that is not really racial. That's just an excuse to be nasty.
Right, but I've got to agree to that also.
Yeah, I mean, there's some people that are just going to be hateful and hate other people. They're mad at the
world.
They're
not racial connected, sure enough.

and they always going to find some excuse. But I find there's always been different kinds of people than you are. From steady, you know, and they have people who stand by other people. Some people are shy, some people are friendly.

Well, yes, that's a common way of life here in New Orleans. it's been that way as far back as I can remember. But I tell you one thing that I find this that still exists. The loyalty among relatives and close friends and neighbors, that still exists in certain parts. Because just for instance, if a neighbor say there's someone taken sick in the family, it wouldn't be ten minutes before half of the neighborhood being there trying to see what they could do. Which I think is great. And for instance, my grandmother was a midwife. And I guess my grandmother brought more white people in the world than she did me was. As a politician here, I was raised up with his name a scammer. But my grandmother brought him into the world and she brought all of his kids. The hatred and the prejudices, I don't think existed as much in those days, but the little frictions were there.

Well, of course, at that time, the laws were different before your time anyway. marriage. And I've had a very hard time explaining that to people. You can talk to somebody who's young and they don't know how much change because I talked to these old people and they remember when intermarriage was a legal thing in this state. Racial intermarriage. We're about to run out of tape.
Well, you mean it was legal.
It was legal.
Right.
Yeah.
A lot of it was just marriage on the paper, in the sight, not written down and recorded by an authority. It just lived together. Yeah.
Yeah, well, that's in your time, but I think there was a lot more marriage and of course, in those times, it was nothing to jump the fence. That happened all the time.
Yeah, it still happens.
It's still today. It's going
to continue to happen because a man always is seeking some place where he can have peace and happiness. .

I don't want to put my name down before. My name is Dick Allen and this is the second reel of Don Alba and today is May the 27th, 1972. Right. I believe, okay. Let's see, what we're talking about. We're talking about the rise of the segregation laws, the Jim Crow laws and how people were married legally. Interracial marriages took place and they didn't have, at one point they didn't have segregation on the streetcars here.
That came on in the later years.
Do you remember that?
I remember when the cars became segregated, but I can't recall when they were not.
Yeah. Well, I just...

Well, as they say, New Orleans was a melting pot and that's a good name to give it. Because in my wife's family, they're Filipinos, they're Chinamans, and they're various other races. And then, I remember the Turks were here. They were people that were dog-skinned, reddish complexion, with jet black string hair, beautiful. And they're intermarried and if you notice around New Orleans, they can find a lot of these fellow clown hair. But that type of hair, that complexion, they call them a nickname, Turk. Well, that's where they come from, that intermarriage there.

Well, you know, at one time they had a lot of Turkish tunes out, you know, American songs, but with Turkish tones, flavor to them. That's right. And Chinese flavor and all that. And I wondered why. People here liked them. Maybe that had something to do with it?
I guess it has.
Well, you still hear people called Turk and Chinese. I hear that Chinese is very common and Dutch, you said, their sister is called Dutch.
They call them that because of their background or their looks, their physical looks.
Yeah.
And then nationally, they do have that part of blood in them that comes from that type of people.
Nobody thought anything about calling anybody anything like that then?
No, no, they never did.
No insults. No insults.
No insults. If it was a little nickname, it wasn't an insulting name.
Well, did you get out of town before you played music, before you became a musician? Did you go anywhere out of town? Well, you mean traveling?

Yeah. No. I never was able to travel. My people were poor people. And we didn't have any money traveling. Well, I didn't start to travel until I learned how to play. And I was playing on the Sesquahanna and I thought that was the longest trip that I could ever make. Crossing Lake Punch and Train from Spanish Falls to the other side of the lake. And I thought that was about the height of my travel career then. Well, now you can cross Lake Punch and Train in five or ten minutes. And I thought that was a great place.
Well, what was it like on the other side? Beautiful.

I can remember the trees and the green shrubbery. A few homes. Beautiful homes sitting in these, under these great big trees. Of course, you had the slum area over there. Well, now I wouldn't say slum. I hate to use it. Yeah. But, for instance, Buddy B.T. lived in the great trumpet players about 25, 30 years ahead of time. He lived in the little one room shack and he took a vacuum to me. And every time I would go to the dock, I'd try to see how fast I could get off of that. And we'd sit down and talk with Buddy. And I'd ask him questions about his horn. And I thought all in all he was a grandfellow. Too bad that there's not too much on the record to preserve what he really done. A lot of credit goes to Buddy B.T. And a lot of credit goes to Buddy B.T. And he deserves it. And people like Buddy B.T. and Kip Renee. And another one that I most certainly have to mention because he was the most beautiful trumpet player and blues player I've ever heard in my life was Chris Kelly. And if you ever listen to Cootie Williams with Duke when Cootie plays with the plunger, Cootie picked this up from Chris Kelly. Well that's one of the things that I wanted to talk to you about.
One of the things I was trying to get in there from a slant and vicular way as a country.
You know?
Like you go over there and you hear Buddy. Is there anybody on the record that sounds like Buddy that you've ever heard?

Not that I can recall right now. But I tell you what. Punch Miller, when Punch was young, he copied Buddy B.T. style as close as he could. But today, no I can't say that I, well, if you listen to my records, you'll hear a trumpet player named Billy Douglas. I think Billy Douglas is one of the greatest trumpet players I've ever heard in my life. Technical. The tonation wasn't the best in the world, but as a technical trumpet player, making things that we musicians hear are almost impossible, you get a vivid idea of what I'm trying to say about Punch and about Buddy. It was a variation style that these guys played. Well then you come along with Louis, and now you have a different vein all together. Louis didn't fingers harm too much as people say, on certain numbers, yes. But his mostly was from what he felt within himself, which made quite a difference. That's the difference in musicians playing music today, and musicians playing music in the olden days. Well, a lot of people say you're old-timing. Well, maybe I am old-timing. But the fact still remains within me such that if I listen to something, I want to enjoy it. And these guys brought out of their souls on their instruments, looking at you and you looking at them, and it was communication there of happiness. Which today I imagine to some people is happiness, but I don't see too much happiness when I look in the crowd.
Do you think the musicians are a hack of the play of that kind of music?

What kind of music are we talking about? The ones that play? No, maybe the young ones, that's all they know. The thing about it is this, that these young musicians have never been exposed to real good bands. Big bands. Big bands. Big bands started this band in 1940 because of the depression that was almost coming back. And they weren't in demand. So, take my band for instance, I stopped in 1940 because there wasn't too much money, there wasn't too many dates, and things like that. But these young musicians never heard these things. So, they don't know.
Yeah, well the only time they hear is a few seconds on television. That's all.
And that's all very seldom. Well even the big bands today are out in left field. They're trying to do things like the young musicians are doing.
What is tonation?

Tonation is that that you get out of the horns. Like some fellas say, well man his tone sounds like a pea shooter. Another guy says he has a tone bigger round as an apple. Well here's what that means. If a guy plays a horn and he has a light sound coming out, well that's a pea shooter sound. You know you play your own sound like, Alright then if he hears a great big sound like, Look, you say that's a sound as big around as a bowl. Because it's beautiful. It has a space that it's covered. And a pea shooter doesn't cover too much space.
Well now you're talking about blues and Judy Williams and all that. Did you know Lips Fades when you were in fact?
